entry.title: Cooling slowly, and why it grows better crystals

link.title: Cooling slowly, and why it grows better crystals

entry.content:
Demo post — includes real equations so the MathJax rendering can be checked. Fernando will review and replace the text.

In a driven granular layer, the role of temperature is played by the granular temperature, the mean kinetic energy of the velocity fluctuations:

\[T_g \;=\; \frac{1}{d}\,\big\langle\, \lvert \mathbf{v} - \langle \mathbf{v}\rangle \rvert^{2} \,\big\rangle ,\]

with $d$ the number of spatial dimensions. Unlike a real thermostat, $T_g$ is not something we set directly — it is the balance between the power injected by the drive and the power dissipated in inelastic collisions. For a system of $N$ grains that balance can be written

\[\frac{d}{dt}\!\left( \tfrac{1}{2} N d\, T_g \right) \;=\; P_{\text{in}} \;-\; \Gamma\, T_g^{3/2},\]

where the loss term $\Gamma\,T_g^{3/2}$ is the standard Haff form for a cooling granular gas. Setting the left-hand side to zero gives the quasi-steady temperature the layer sits at for a given drive, $T_g^{\ast} = \left(P_{\text{in}}/\Gamma\right)^{2/3}$.

Whether the layer orders is then governed by a single dimensionless group,

\[\Pi \;=\; \frac{T_g^{\ast}}{\varepsilon_{\text{cage}}},\]

the ratio of the granular temperature to the energy $\varepsilon_{\text{cage}}$ needed to break out of the cage of nearest neighbors. For $\Pi \gg 1$ the grains diffuse freely; for $\Pi \lesssim 1$ they are trapped. Crystals nucleate and grow in the narrow window just above $\Pi \simeq 1$: cold enough to be ordered, still warm enough for particles to find their lattice sites.

Why “staggered”

If you ramp the drive down in one smooth sweep, the layer races through that window and quenches into a glass. Instead we cut $P_{\text{in}}$ in steps, holding at each level for a waiting time $\tau_w$ long enough for the local order parameter

\[\psi_6(\mathbf{r}) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} e^{\,i\,6\theta_{j}}\]

to relax before the next cut. Here $\theta_j$ is the angle of the bond to the $j$-th of $n$ neighbors, and $\lvert \psi_6 \rvert \to 1$ in a perfect triangular lattice. Optimizing the schedule is then a trade-off: too short a $\tau_w$ and disorder is frozen in; too long and you have merely wasted time. In our experiments the best final $\langle \lvert \psi_6 \rvert \rangle$ came from a handful of steps with $\tau_w$ of order the structural relaxation time at each stage — the granular echo of annealing a real crystal.
entry.summary: A short walk through the physics of staggered cooling in a non-vibrating granular system, equations included.

entry.title: A bowl of beads as a stand-in for matter

link.title: A bowl of beads as a stand-in for matter

entry.content:
Demo post — written to show tone and formatting. Fernando will review and replace.

Atoms in a liquid are too small and too fast to film. A colloidal particle in water is already a big improvement — micrometers across, slow enough for a microscope — but still fiddly. So in our lab we go one step further and use millimeter-sized grains: glass spheres, plastic cubes, steel beads. You can hold them in your hand, and a normal camera resolves every single one.

The catch is that grains do not move on their own. Left alone they just sit there, losing energy to friction at every contact. To make them behave like a “thermal” system we have to feed energy in continuously — by vibrating the container, tilting it, blowing air through it, or, in the magnetic case, switching an external field on and off. Turn the driving off and everything freezes in place. That single difference — energy in, energy out, never at equilibrium — is what makes granular matter its own field, and also what makes it such a revealing model.

What the model buys us

Once the grains are fluidized, familiar phenomena show up at a scale we can watch frame by frame:

  • Crystallization: cool the driving slowly and the grains settle into ordered lattices, with the same kinds of defects and grain boundaries seen in real solids.
  • The glass transition: cool it too fast and they jam into a disordered, rigid state instead.
  • Melting and superheating: a granular crystal can be pushed past its melting point and stay ordered for a while, just like an overheated solid.
  • Active matter: give each grain a way to convert the driving into self-propulsion and you get flocking, clustering, and lane formation.

None of this proves anything about atoms by itself. What it does is let us see the mechanism — which particle moved first, where the ordered region nucleated, how a defect traveled — and then ask whether the same story holds for systems we can only measure indirectly.

The one number that matters

Whether the grains explore their landscape or get stuck comes down to a ratio: how much energy the driving delivers per particle versus how much it costs to rearrange a cage of neighbors. When that ratio is large, the pile flows and orders; when it drops below roughly one, motion arrests. A slow, staggered cooling schedule keeps the system just above that threshold for as long as possible — and, in our experiments, that is exactly when the best crystals grow. The next post works through that idea with a bit of math.
entry.summary: Why we shake, tilt and magnetize grains to learn about atoms we can never watch directly.
